newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Six-month lead outlook bearish, Mocatta says.
newsitem.headline: Six-month lead outlook bearish, Mocatta says.

text.p: The lead market, until recently a darling of the London Metal Exchange (LME), is in for a rough six months as the fundamental and technical outlooks turn bearish, trading firm Mocatta Base Metals said on Monday in a report.
"We cannot find anything bullish for the market," Mocatta, a division of Standard Chartered Bank Australia Ltd, said.
Lead climbed to a recent high of US$733 a tonne in mid-January, largely on speculative buying on the back of a firmer zinc market.
But lead prices quickly receded as European-based liquidation selling ignited a downward run, Mocatta noted.
Three-month lead closed LME trading at US$680 a tonne last Friday.

Despite industry figures pointing to a supply deficit of 166,000 tonnes in 1996, evidence suggests that current consumption is being outstripped by increasing production, with stocks rising steadily over the year, Mocatta said.
International Lead and Zinc Study Group figures show world lead consumption rose 2.3 percent to 5.7 million tonnes in 1996 while lead production fell 1.4 percent to 5.53 million tonnes.
Production in the Commonwealth of Independent States is gradually recovering, Mocatta said.
But this is being accompanied by a sharp downturn in local consumption and increasing amounts of Russian exports to Western markets, the trading firm said.
"Underscoring this bearish outlook is disappointing demand for lead, particularly in light of the harsh European winter," Mocatta said.
Cold winters prove wearing on lead-bearing vehicle batteries, resulting in expectations of a high number of replacements, thus boosting lead's demand potential.
The technical prospects for lead are also poor, Mocatta said.
"Despite a brief respite from mid-December, the short-term moving averages have recrossed bearishly, running parallel on the descent," it said.
A downtrend channel, started in May 1996, remains well-established, it added.

"The speculative rally during January surprised many trade customers, both in magnitude and timing," Mocatta said. "The strength of other metals and the belief that metal remained tight helped promote this move."
Mocatta said it now believes such sentiment was misplaced and that for at least the next six months the market will be a bearish one
Looking back, Mocatta said the rally to US$730 a tonne was a "classic selling opportunity."
